note: Per-claim evidence layer, v1 (September 2026). Each factual claim in a gap's dossier is listed with its sources, a status and a last-verified date. Statuses: verified (checked against the cited source), reported (attributed to a named organisation's publication), estimate (a modelled or approximate figure, labelled as such), source-to-confirm (stated in the dossier with primary attribution pending, queued for the next review pass). The prose dossier stays the reading layer; this is the audit layer. Coverage grows tier by tier, build-now entries first. Method kin: Discourse Graphs.

claims.claim: From April 2026, around 379 Pride in Place neighbourhood boards begin spending up to £20m each.
The 2026 Act obliges councils to establish neighbourhood governance arrangements.
Local Trust winds down in 2026; its Community Leadership Academy supported leaders across 150 Big Local areas and helped mobilise more than 6,000 first-time volunteers.
The government's community organiser training programmes ended years ago.
JRF has flagged capacity as the Pride in Place programme's key risk.
No body is charged with training, peer networks or governance support for the incoming resident decision-makers.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: mySociety runs TheyWorkForYou, WhatDoTheyKnow and FixMyStreet, cross-subsidised through consultancy and short grants.
Democracy Club crowd-sources candidate and results data the state does not publish, and the Electoral Commission is absorbing only the polling-station finder.
mySociety's Shifting Landscapes report of January 2026 concludes there is no systematic support for public-interest technology in the UK.
Careful Industries reaches the same conclusion about the absence of systematic support.
Germany's Sovereign Tech Fund pays for maintenance of critical open infrastructure.
claims.note: The fund's own publications are cited on gap 13; the cross-reference should be added here directly. Queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: Grant funders prefer novelty over maintenance, leaving load-bearing civic services one funding cycle from shutdown.
Citizens UK has 19 chapters and over 100 staff, funded by member dues, project grants and a Lottery Solidarity Fund award of about £5m over nine years.
ACORN's dues-funded model sustains branches in around ten cities.
The state's Community Organisers Programme trained 500 organisers between 2011 and 2015 and ended without succession.
Foundations fund organising mainly through short project grants that conflict with the model's need for patient core money.
No UK equivalent exists of the dedicated organising philanthropy intermediaries of the US.
claims.note: The Civic Power Fund is the nascent UK exception; the claim holds at US scale and the wording needs sharpening at the October 2026 review.

claims.claim: The EU's Next Generation Internet initiative distributed around €140m to more than 1,200 projects in small cascade grants, largely through NLnet.
The Commission dropped NGI from the Horizon Europe 2025 work programme.
UK civil-society funders treat technology as unfundable infrastructure, and the Nesta and National Lottery digital funds have closed.
No domestic substitute exists at the €5k to €50k grant size where most independent maintainers live.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: GOV.UK Notify serves more than 1,500 public services and explicitly excludes charities, community pharmacies, hospices, housing associations and universities.
Notify's code is open source.
claims.note: True and easily shown; the alphagov repository should be cited directly. Queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: Charities re-buy messaging, forms and payments at retail SaaS prices with donated funds.
No UK body provides equivalent shared digital infrastructure to civil society.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: The EU Cyber Resilience Act creates obligations for manufacturers and an open-source-software-steward category, phasing in through 2026-27.
UK-based foundations, SMEs and maintainers whose software reaches the EU market must comply regardless of Brexit.
The UK's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, at report stage in June 2026, focuses on NIS-regulated sectors and makes no provision for open source stewardship.
claims.note: The stewardship point is an absence claim, verified by reading the bill documents for such provision and finding none.

claims.claim: No UK-facing CRA compliance help for maintainers exists.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: The British Youth Council, the UK's youth-led representative umbrella since 1948, went insolvent in March 2024 when its backer entered administration.
DCMS moved Youth Parliament delivery to the National Youth Agency as a government-contracted arrangement.
BYC's federating, Youth Select Committee and European Youth Forum representation functions have no successor.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: The UK is now one of very few European democracies without an independent national youth council.
claims.note: A comparative claim; the European Youth Forum's membership list is the checkable source to cite. Queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: The National Citizen Service closed in March 2025 after over £1bn spent since 2011, cutting funding to around 250 delivery organisations.
The replacement programmes are place-based provision for disadvantaged areas rather than a universal mixing-and-service experience.
NCVO's Time Well Spent research shows youth-relevant participation roughly halving since 2018.
France runs the SNU and the US runs AmeriCorps, and the UK now has no national civic service pathway.
claims.note: The comparative half needs direct citations to the SNU and AmeriCorps programmes; the UK absence was checked in July 2026. Queued for the October review pass.

claims.claim: The Centre for Social Justice's Lost Boys work documents male NEET numbers up 40 per cent since the pandemic, against 7 per cent for women.
Suicide is the leading cause of death for young men aged 15 to 19.
claims.note: Cited via CSJ, which draws on official mortality statistics; the direct ONS citation should be added at the October 2026 review.

claims.claim: John Smith Centre polling finds young men markedly more right-leaning and distrustful than young women.
No UK funder runs a dedicated programme for young men's civic participation, while Rosa and the Tampon Tax legacy funds exist for women and girls.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: 61.5 per cent of young people get political information mainly from social media, and 73 per cent signed a petition or advocated online in the past year.
The Electoral Commission's Welcome to Your Vote Week is a school-focused education programme.
Party youth wings are actively recruiting, with Reform launching a student wing and the Conservatives relaunching theirs.
No at-scale nonpartisan registration-and-turnout operation exists in the UK.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: The Scouts' waiting list passed 100,000 in 2024.
claims.note: Currently cited to an encyclopedia entry; the Scout Association's own annual report is the primary source to substitute. Queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: Girlguiding and the Scouts run joint growth projects, and both face adult-volunteer constraints.
Overall volunteering has declined since the pandemic.
No national mechanism recruits, trains or gives employer time-off entitlements to adult volunteers for youth movements.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: HS2 Phase 1 costs about £396m per mile against about £46m for comparable French high-speed lines, and Britain Remade's dataset of 138 transit and 104 road projects across 14 countries shows UK costs running two to eight times EU peers.
The Lower Thames Crossing consent alone cost about £300m.
NISTA's pipeline portal lists projects and values rather than standardised outturn unit costs, and the pipeline is worth £718bn.
Under the May 2025 Mansion House Accord, seventeen providers pledged 10 per cent of DC default funds to private markets by 2030, with 5 per cent in the UK.
claims.note: Recapped in the cited legal analysis; the Accord's own text is the primary source to add at the October 2026 review.

claims.claim: The Pension Schemes Act 2026 holds a backstop mandation power exercisable once between 2028 and 2032.
The British Growth Partnership's first fund closed at £200m, with Aegon UK, NatWest Cushon and M&G participating.
Few long-term asset funds offer UK venture or growth exposure at institutional scale.
claims.note: A market-scan assessment from the July 2026 research pass.

claims.claim: The OBR's 2025 Fiscal Risks and Sustainability report projects public debt at 274 per cent of GDP by the early 2070s on its baseline.
The OBR is statutorily barred from recommending policy.
claims.note: The bar sits in the Budget Responsibility and National Audit Act 2011, section 5. Add the legislation.gov.uk citation.

claims.claim: The UK borrows around £300bn gross a year, and roughly a quarter of the gilt stock is index-linked.
claims.note: Both figures track the DMO's published remit and portfolio statistics; add the DMO remit page as the primary source.

claims.claim: The 2022 LDI episode caught official contingency planning out and nearly broke the pension system, at a cost of billions.
claims.note: Exhaustively documented, but the entry cites no source for it. The Bank of England's LDI post-mortem in its Financial Stability Report is the primary source to add.

claims.claim: No public body or institute runs publicly war-gamed sovereign stress scenarios with pre-agreed response playbooks.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked against OBR publications (risk identification only, no playbooks), the Lords Economic Affairs Committee inquiry, and the public output of IFS, NIESR and the Resolution Foundation.

claims.claim: Term premia run at roughly double historic norms and the marginal gilt buyer is a leveraged hedge fund.
claims.note: Academic and sell-side analysis; the Goldman Sachs piece is a conflicted source the entry itself names as such.

claims.claim: 30-year gilt term premia reached 2.45 per cent in 2025 against a long-run average of 1.06 per cent.
UK households cannot buy gilts directly from the state; purchases route through brokers and platforms, and the DMO's approved-group retail access is vestigial.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked against the DMO's own description of gilt purchase routes and the NS&I product range, which sells its own savings products rather than gilts.

claims.claim: US TreasuryDirect and Italy's retail BTP programmes raised tens of billions from households and stabilised demand.
claims.note: Italy's BTP Valore issues each raised over €15bn; the Italian Treasury's own results announcements and TreasuryDirect holdings data are the primary sources to add.

claims.claim: UK debt interest runs at £126bn a year.
claims.note: The OBR's Economic and Fiscal Outlook is the primary source to add; the figure moves with each forecast round.

claims.claim: Defined-benefit pension run-off has removed the DMO's captive long-dated buyer and shortened issuance.
Oflog was abolished in December 2024.
claims.note: Currently resting on an encyclopedia entry plus trade press. MHCLG's own announcement of the abolition is the primary source to substitute.

claims.claim: The Local Audit Office created by the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act carries no continuous financial-resilience monitoring mandate.
claims.note: Checked against the Act's functions clauses; the LAO's remit is audit-market oversight.

claims.claim: 41 per cent of council accounts received disclaimed opinions in the latest backstop round, and 22 councils missed the March 2026 deadline.
claims.note: The 41 per cent figure is government-published; the 22-council count is LGC reporting.

claims.claim: Local authority debt stands at a record £154.6bn.
claims.note: Currently cited to a campaign group's briefing. The underlying data is DLUHC/MHCLG borrowing and investment statistics; substitute the official series at review.

claims.claim: 30 councils received Exceptional Financial Support in 2025-26, and fourteen have gone effectively bankrupt via section 114 notices.
claims.note: MHCLG publishes the EFS awards list; add it, plus a section 114 tracker for the cumulative count.

claims.claim: No timely, comparable public dataset of council financial resilience exists; CIPFA's resilience index is annual, lagged and voluntary.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked against the CIPFA index's own methodology, the paused early-warning conversations pilot, and the new local outcomes framework, which measures service outcomes rather than balance-sheet risk.

claims.claim: The landmark UK surveillance cases, including Bridges v South Wales, the bulk-powers tribunal challenges and the Apple/Privacy International case, were brought by a handful of small organisations.
claims.note: The organisations' own case pages establish who brought each action.

claims.claim: The Digital Freedom Fund makes litigation grants Europe-wide and cannot anchor a UK pipeline.
claims.note: DFF's own funding criteria page is the source to add; the UK-pipeline judgment is the entry's inference from its grant scope.

claims.claim: The EHRC joined the Met facial recognition judicial review in August 2025 and does not originate surveillance cases.
claims.note: The EHRC's own press release on the intervention is the primary source to add.

claims.claim: No costs-capping protection comparable to the Aarhus environmental rules exists for public-interest data cases, and no legal aid covers them.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked against Civil Procedure Rules 46.24-46.28, which confine costs caps to Aarhus Convention environmental claims, and LASPO legal aid scope.

claims.claim: These cases run on crowdfunding and a few foundation grants, with the claimant organisations carrying adverse-costs risk.
The main UK digital rights organisations run on budgets of roughly £0.5m to £2m each.
claims.note: Currently resting on encyclopedia entries. The organisations' filed accounts at the Charity Commission and Companies House are the primary sources to substitute.

claims.claim: The funder set is concentrated and largely non-domestic: JRRT, Luminate, Open Society Foundations and the Sigrid Rausing Trust dominate the sector's grant income.
claims.note: Established from the funders' and grantees' own published grant listings.

claims.claim: No UK pooled fund, endowment or community-foundation stream for digital rights exists on the Civitates or Ford/MacArthur model.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked against the Funding Justice 3 landscape annex, which maps UK justice and rights funders and shows no pooled digital rights vehicle.

claims.claim: The sector's whole annual budget runs under £15m.
claims.note: Summed from the named organisations' accounts. A worked table belongs in the review pass so the total is reproducible.

claims.claim: A single funder exit can remove a quarter of an organisation's income.
claims.note: Follows from the concentration visible in ORG's own funder list; the OSF restructuring is the live example.

claims.claim: No UK equivalent of the EFF's Atlas of Surveillance exists.
claims.note: Absence claim. The Atlas covers US agencies only; checked for a UK register across the ICO, Home Office, the Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner's legacy publications and academic projects. Nothing maintained and machine-readable exists.

claims.claim: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard is mandatory for central departments, while police compliance stays patchy.
claims.note: The gov.uk ATRS mandate announcement and the published record counts are the primary sources to add.

claims.claim: Live facial recognition deployment data is published inconsistently force by force.
Procurement of tools like Facewatch and mobile recognition apps surfaces only through FOI investigations.
The Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025 lets DWP require banks to scan benefit claimants' accounts through Eligibility Verification Notices.
Rollout begins in 2026 on a test-and-learn basis.
The codes of practice governing the powers were finalised in May 2026.
The Information Commissioner raised concerns about the eligibility verification measure during the Bill's passage.
Neither the Act's review mechanisms nor the codes of practice require independent publication of error and false-positive rates.
claims.note: An absence claim: verified by reading the cited documents for such a requirement and finding none.

claims.claim: Roughly ten million accounts fall within the scope of the screening.
claims.note: A widely cited civil-society estimate of accounts in scope. Primary attribution is pending and queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: DWP has documented bias problems in its fraud models.
claims.note: Refers to DWP's own machine-learning fairness disclosures as reported at the time. The primary disclosure document needs citing directly; queued for the October 2026 review pass.

claims.claim: No independent body or civil-society observatory monitors notice volumes or outcomes, and JUSTICE's published analysis covered the Bill rather than the rollout.
claims.note: An absence claim, checked by search during the July 2026 research pass; the JUSTICE briefing is cited as the sector's closest published work.

claims.claim: The Procurement Act debarment regime went live on 24 February 2025 and the published list remains blank, by its own statement, until a minister decides to add a supplier.
The first debarment investigations, into cladding suppliers named in the Grenfell Inquiry report, were paused in July 2025 at the request of the CPS and the Metropolitan Police.
claims.note: The Cabinet Office written ministerial statement announcing the pause is the primary source to add.

claims.claim: The Covid Counter-Fraud Commissioner put total Covid scheme fraud and error at £10.9bn, with £1.8bn recovered.

The debarment function acts only on referral from contracting authorities and ministerial discretion, with no statutory timelines and no third-party trigger; it was absorbed into the Government Commercial Agency in April 2026.
claims.note: The referral-and-discretion design is in the published guidance. The April 2026 absorption into the GCA lacks its own citation; add the machinery-of-government announcement.

claims.claim: Nobody runs systematic corruption red-flag monitoring across the Central Digital Platform's procurement data.
claims.note: Absence claim. Tussell provides commercial analytics for sales intelligence; checked for an integrity-focused equivalent across Transparency International UK, Spotlight on Corruption and the Open Contracting Partnership's UK work.

claims.claim: The ECCTA anti-SLAPP provisions came into force on 18 June 2025 and apply only to claims relating to economic crime.
In March 2026 the High Court delivered the first statutory anti-SLAPP strike-out, dismissing an £8m libel claim in Kamal v Tax Policy Associates.
claims.note: Two independent secondary accounts agree; the judgment's neutral citation on the National Archives case law service is the primary source to add.

claims.claim: The government has stated it has no current plans to extend anti-SLAPP protection beyond economic crime.
claims.note: The statement exists in ministerial answers; the Hansard reference is the primary source to add.

claims.claim: The UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition has a drafted model law ready.
Journalism is not a recognised charitable purpose under the Charities Act, and Full Fact was rejected twice before securing charitable status.
claims.note: The legal position is set out by the Charitable Journalism Project and charity-law practitioners; the Charity Commission's published decisions on Full Fact would make it primary.

claims.claim: The UK lost a net 265 local newspaper titles between 2005 and 2020.
claims.note: The figure originates in Press Gazette's local news count; add that research directly.

claims.claim: The Public Interest News Foundation is the only UK charity dedicated to regenerating local news.
claims.note: Absence claim resting on PINF's own positioning; checked the charity register for competitors with the same object and found none.

claims.claim: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Finance Uncovered depend on fragile, largely overseas philanthropy.
claims.note: Both publish funder lists; add them so the overseas weighting is checkable.

claims.claim: The cheapest FCA society registration at £40 is conditional on using a sponsoring body's model rules, which are charged for.
claims.note: The FCA's own fee table ties the lowest registration fee to model rules from a sponsoring body.

claims.claim: Formation knowledge is scattered across sponsoring bodies, law-firm briefings and volunteer wikis, with model rules behind paywalls.
No openly licensed, maintained, versioned corpus of UK formation templates exists.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked Co-operatives UK, Cwmpas, the Plunkett Foundation, Community Shares Unit and law-clinic publication lists; each publishes fragments, none an open versioned library.

claims.claim: Withdrawable community shares are exempt from prospectus and financial-promotion regulation, and protection rests on the voluntary Standard Mark run by Co-operatives UK.
Law Commission consultation paper 264 proposed statutory share definitions, prescribed withdrawal conditions, write-down protections and interest caps, with the final report expected in 2026.
Community shares drew over £1m of match-crowded investment through the Booster Fund in 2025, a record year.
claims.note: Programme-operator figures; the Booster Fund is Co-operatives UK's own scheme.

claims.claim: No secondary market or underwriting facility exists for community shares; withdrawal depends entirely on a society's cash position.
claims.note: Absence claim. The Law Commission consultation paper documents the withdrawal mechanism and the lack of any transfer market.

claims.claim: Roughly 300 small volunteer-run forums exited or migrated when the OSA illegal-content duties began in March 2025, with at least 22 confirmed closures on Neil Brown's tracker.
claims.note: The 22 confirmed closures come from the tracker's own author; the ~300 figure is his wider estimate of exits and migrations. Cite the tracker on onlinesafetyact.co.uk directly at review.

claims.claim: LFGSS and Microcosm announced shutdown over the Act's duties and only partially returned.
claims.note: The operator's own shutdown announcement.

claims.claim: Ofcom offers a small-services hub and compliance guide, but every volunteer admin must still individually produce risk assessments.
A December 2025 Westminster Hall debate aired the small-services burden without resolution.
claims.note: Cited to a Hansard mirror; swap to the hansard.parliament.uk record at review.

claims.claim: No compliance mutual, group insurance product or shared template compliance stack exists for community-run services.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked Ofcom's small-services resources, ORG's campaign output, and the specialist insurance market; nothing offers pooled legal defence or model risk assessments as a service.

claims.claim: Section 121 of the Online Safety Act lets Ofcom mandate accredited scanning technology for private messaging, and Ofcom finalised its Technology Notices guidance in May 2026.
Enforcement against end-to-end encrypted services is deferred only by a ministerial assurance on technical feasibility, which has no legal force.
claims.note: The assurance was given in the Lords in September 2023; the Hansard record is the primary source to add, and the Proton account is an interested party's.

claims.claim: Apple withdrew Advanced Data Protection from UK users in February 2025, and the tribunal litigation ended after the Home Office narrowed its order to UK users.
Privacy International's challenge to the secrecy of technical capability notices was heard in 2026.
claims.note: The claimant's own case page.

claims.claim: No statutory transparency reporting on IPA technical capability notices exists, not even aggregate counts, and no dedicated UK encryption defence fund backs small providers.
claims.note: Absence claim. Checked the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 reporting provisions and IPCO annual reports, which disclose nothing on TCNs; ORG, PI and Big Brother Watch fund encryption work from general budgets.
